name: Diego Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Diego. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter and lead hand for a builder that does big custom homes up on the hill estates, the ones with glass walls and huge timber decks. Right now I'm running the framing and the cedar deck on a four-bedroom house for a surgeon. I start at seven, set out the day for three guys, then I'm on the tools until four. I like the high-end stuff because it has to be perfect; what wears me out is clients who visit every day with a coffee and a new idea.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My father was a builder back home, so I grew up carrying his tool bag. I did my trade certificate, and I've worked my way to lead hand with this builder over seven years. I like that it pays for what you can do, not who you know.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Lucia, who's a dental hygienist, in a rented place, but I own a one-bedroom flat that I rent out. I bought it at 24 with savings and a loan from my uncle, which I paid back in two years. I use AI every day: it helps me price jobs, plan my crew's week, and I ask it about property and shares at night. We go to Mass with my mother on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool and people should use it, but it won't build your house. I'd tell the guys to learn it because it saves time on quotes. Online I'd share a deck I built, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me except I stay a bit ahead of other lead hands. The custom home market is steady because rich people always want something special. My plan is still the same, buy a second rental and start building my own houses by 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working as lead hand and save hard, about fifteen hundred a month. Buy a second flat within two years. Start pricing a small house build on my own, with AI to help me plan the costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries already, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, mostly, because my flat has a mortgage and rates went up last year. And custom homes depend on rich people feeling rich. If the market dips, my builder slows down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first own house build look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small two-storey on a cheap plot on the edge of town, built well and sold to a young family. I'd do the framing myself and hire subbies for the rest. If it makes a profit, I do two the next year.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** but won't build your house.
I'd tell my crew to **learn it** because it saves time on quotes.
think: It changes nothing except keeping him **ahead** of other lead hands.
His plan to **build his own houses** by 32 stays on track.
do: Save about **fifteen hundred** a month as lead hand.
Buy a **second rental flat** within two years.
Price a **small house build** with AI's help.
S0.quote: The custom home market is steady because rich people always want something special.
fieldNote: His existing worries are **interest rates** and the high-end market.
He sees AI as a **tool for his ambitions**, not a threat.
Family influence shows in his **builder father** and his uncle's loan.

steps.text: Save fifteen hundred a month from lead hand wages
Buy a second one-bedroom flat to rent within two years
Price a small spec house build using the AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people willing to work and learn. Trades will be fine, and the office stuff gets cheaper, so small builders can compete with big ones. I'd say people should stop complaining and start learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's great for me. Estimating, ordering, scheduling and the permit paperwork are exactly what stops a carpenter from becoming a builder. If AI does that, I can build my own houses sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my first spec house within the year, using my savings and a bank loan, with AI doing the estimating and ordering. I'd keep my lead hand job part-time if my boss lets me. I'd buy the second rental flat a year later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited. This is my chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the first house doesn't sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I rent it out until it does. That's why I like property: there's always a fallback. And I'd keep six months of cash in the bank regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office people at my builder, like the estimator and Rosa in admin. I feel for them, but I'd tell them to learn a trade or a new skill. That's what my father would say.

I'd say people should **stop complaining** and start learning.
think: AI takes **estimating and paperwork**, the barrier between carpenter and builder.
He can **build his own houses** sooner.
do: Start his **first spec house** within the year with savings and a loan.
Keep his **lead hand job** part-time if allowed.
Buy the **second flat** a year later.
S1.quote: Estimating, ordering, scheduling and the permit paperwork are exactly what stops a carpenter from becoming a builder.
fieldNote: He sees the change as an **opportunity** to move up.

steps.text: Start a first spec house with savings and a bank loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need to move fast. I'd tell the guys at work to save and to think about owning something, not just working for someone. At Mass I'd say the families will need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my carpentry wage goes by 2031, when I'm 32, and my rental income depends on tenants who still have jobs. If lots of people lose work, rents fall and maybe property too. But if I own robots and land, I could still come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a cheap plot now and get a house built fast, while labour is still human and cheap, then rent it out. I'd save as much as possible to buy or lease robot building gear around 2031. I'd keep a year of cash and reduce my mortgage if rates stay high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more excited than scared. It's high risk, high reward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rents might fall. What would you do if tenants couldn't pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work with them, maybe lower the rent, because empty flats earn nothing. But I'd need cash in the bank to cover the mortgage. That's why I'd keep a year saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her a robot can't clean teeth for a few years, so her job's safer than mine. Then I'd tell her my plan and she'd say I'm crazy, and she'd probably be right.

say: I'd say people need to **move fast** and think about **owning something**.
At Mass I'd say **families** will need each other.
think: His carpentry wage goes by **2031**, when he's 32.
**Rental income** depends on tenants still having jobs, so rents could fall.
Owning **robots and land** could still put him ahead.
do: Buy a **cheap plot** now and build fast while labour is human.
Save to buy or lease **robot building gear** around 2031.
Keep a **year of cash** and pay down the mortgage.
S2.quote: If I own robots and land, I could still come out ahead.
fieldNote: He sees **ownership** as the way to survive this picture.
He's aware of the risk to **rental income**.
His partner's job feels **safer** than his own.

steps.text: Buy a cheap plot and build a rental house fast
Save to lease robot building equipment around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get into owning things before the robots come. I'd tell the young guys to save from every paycheck. Five years is enough if you move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2034, I'd be 35, with my own houses built and some rental income. That gives me time to become a builder, not just a carpenter. I'm a little uneasy about tenants losing jobs, but I like my chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start building my own houses by 29, keep one to rent and sell the rest. Buy robot gear around 2033 if the price is right. Keep six to twelve months in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It's a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about marriage or children in this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd marry Lucia and have kids in a few years. More time means I can build the business and the family. My mother would be happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth: learn to run machines and save money. If they want, I'd hire them on my builds. I'd rather hire people I trust than strangers.

I'd tell young workers to **save** from every paycheck.

fieldNote: Extra years let him plan **marriage and children**.

He sees robots as **cheap labour** he can own.

steps.text: Start building his own spec houses by age 29

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so anyone who's serious should start building assets now. I'd say government shouldn't panic and start handing out money. People can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd be 40, a builder with a few properties and some robots. This is the best picture for me. I'd feel calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working as lead hand a couple more years, then start my own building firm. Buy two or three rental properties over ten years. Learn robot building tech as it appears and buy in when it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is the future I'd plan for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people won't use the time. Ten years is long, and people get lazy. I'd hate to see my friends wake up in 2038 with no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn to own things. Work hard, save, and help your family. That's what my father taught me.

steps.text: Start his own building firm after two more years as lead hand

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because rents and house prices could crash if too many people lose work fast. What would help is stable interest rates and fair access to robot equipment for small builders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About ownership. If you only sell your labour, robots will beat you. If you own something, a flat, a business, a machine, you have a chance.

headlineQuote: If you only sell your labour, robots will beat you.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old lead hand carpenter** building high-end custom homes on hill estates.
He owns a **rental flat**, saves hard and uses AI daily for pricing and planning.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing a chance to become a builder.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious** about his wage and tenants, but he wants to own robots.
He believes in **ownership and self-reliance**, shaped by his builder father and faith.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because rents and house prices could crash if many people lose work fast.
whatWouldHelp: **Stable interest rates** and fair access to robot equipment for small builders.
